verdict: PERTURB-SEQ AS EDGE EVIDENCE, AND WHAT IT DOES TO PRECISION. The previous module used Perturb-seq only as a whole-profile cosine, discarding the most direct signal available: knocking out A and watching B's transcript. Measured before building, that signal is real -- mean |z| of B under A's knockout is 0.109 on PPI edges against 0.019 on random pairs (5.7x), and 'either direction moves more than 1sd' is 5.99% against 0.49% (12.2x). 1296 of 1400 knockouts are themselves measured genes, so it was computable all along. ON PRECISION, WHICH IS THE NUMBER THAT MATTERS: over the full deployment pool of 965,524 candidate pairs at a 0.3567% base rate, topology alone gets p@100 0.990 and topology plus spatial plus Perturb-seq gets 1.000 (+0.010); at 1000 it is 0.943 -> 0.955. Perturb-seq alone, with no graph and no annotation, reaches p@100 0.750. IN THE SPARSE REGIME the ordering is what matters rather than the level: at CN=0 topology is pinned at 0.500 by construction, and the best arm is +SPAT+PERT at 0.672 +/- 0.029. WHAT THIS CANNOT SAY. 'Knocking out A changes B's mRNA' is FUNCTIONAL coupling; it is being used to predict a PHYSICAL edge, and the two are not the same thing -- a strong directional effect through three intermediates counts identically to a direct contact. Availability is explicit (104 knockouts are not on the measured panel and get a zero effect with an AVAIL indicator so the model cannot read absence as evidence). The pool is knockout-knockout pairs, and a held-out 'true' edge is one already in a database. One cell line, one split.
